strengths: The paper formalizes a genuinely useful new task — text-driven amodal 3D generation — that addresses a real limitation of feedforward image-to-3D models (observation-overfitting under occlusion), and the framing of decoupled control granularities (rigid for observation, relaxed for prompt) is intuitive and well-motivated.
The method is training-free and plug-and-play, evaluated on two distinct backbones (TRELLIS, SAM3D), which strengthens generality of the claimed gains.

Evaluation effort is substantial for this area: two curated benchmarks (ExtremeOcc-3D with 264 cases, AmbiSem-3D with 21 branching cases), multiple baselines including 2D-edit pipelines and occlusion-aware models, a user study (n=32), component ablations, hyperparameter sensitivity (σ, ρ, N), prior-source ablation (retrieved vs. generated), and an honest failure-mode appendix (Fig. 11).

Quantitative results are consistent across backbones and metrics (e.g., Point-FID 141.48→97.79 on TRELLIS, 100.38→81.11 on SAM3D; CLIPtxt 24.08→27.26) with CLIPimg/LPIPS remaining competitive, supporting the central claim of prompt-following without sacrificing observation fidelity.

The visibility-aware, time-varying fusion mechanism and multi-prior consensus are sensible engineering choices with clear ablation support (visibility mask removal causes the largest drop, 81.1→92.3).
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is weaker than claimed. The 'proof' that low-pass relaxation reduces semantic error rests on Assumptions A.2 (semantic field is band-limited) and A.3 (error is dominated by high frequency) that essentially assert the desired conclusion — the interesting question of whether learned velocity errors actually obey this spectral separation is assumed, not established with any empirical spectral analysis. The Wasserstein bound is a straightforward Gronwall/Lipschitz argument that does not require the filtering result.

There is a significant gap between the analyzed object and the implemented one: the theory analyzes a Gaussian low-pass operator applied directly to the velocity field (Eq. 2), but the implementation blurs cross-attention logits (Eq. 8). The connection is only via an additional Lipschitz assumption (A.11) and a claim of 'analogous relaxation' (Appendix A.4) — the abstract claim in the abstract/intro that the relaxation 'is equivalent to applying a low-pass filter on the generative vector field' is an overstatement.

The formal ODE framework (Eq. 1, oracle/standard/RelaxFlow instantiations) is largely narrative; the actual sampler (Eqs. 9-11) uses a discretized cutoff schedule and spatial visibility masking that do not clearly instantiate the analyzed ODE, weakening the theory-to-practice link.

Evaluation has notable limitations: AmbiSem-3D has only 21 curated cases (user study n=32), making the 68.52% preference figures statistically fragile; FID and Point-FID are computed over very small sample sets; Point-FID with a Point-E encoder as a 'semantic similarity' metric for multi-solution completion is unvalidated; and CLIPtxt gains are modest (~3 points) for a method whose headline claim is prompt steering.

On ExtremeOcc-3D, priors are retrieved from the same 3D-FUTURE dataset as the test objects, raising a mild information-leakage concern (mitigated but not eliminated by the generated-prior ablation at 82.7 vs 81.1).

Several baseline comparisons are somewhat asymmetric: on AmbiSem-3D, occlusion-aware models (SAM3D, Amodal3R) were never designed for prompt-following, so beating them on CLIPtxt is expected; the more meaningful comparisons (2D edit pipelines, multi-view TRELLIS) show smaller margins.

The appendix proofs contain notational inconsistencies (e.g., E_sem defined with c_obs conditioning in Eq. 15 vs. c_sem in Eq. 3; 'Theorem A.7' vs. 'Lemma A.7'; proof of Prop. A.4 refers to 'for a sufficiently small β' with β never defined in the statement), and the main text has typos ('Srutinize', 'Encounter'), suggesting insufficient proofreading for the theoretical sections.
No explicit code or benchmark release is stated, which limits reproducibility of the two new diagnostic benchmarks that are listed as a core contribution.

strengths: The paper formalizes a well-motivated and clearly articulated new task — text-driven amodal 3D generation — that distinguishes observation fidelity from prompt following, and the dual-branch decomposition (rigid observation control vs. relaxed semantic steering) is a sensible and clearly motivated design.
The method is training-free and plug-and-play, instantiated on two strong backbones (TRELLIS and SAM3D), which supports generality of the approach.

The experimental protocol includes ablations of every major component (low-pass relaxation, visibility mask, cutoff schedule, prior source, prior count), and qualitative results across many categories support the claim that intent steering works without destroying visible evidence.

The authors introduce two diagnostic benchmarks with documented curation procedures, and provide an honest failure-case analysis (Appendix G, Fig. 11) describing soft concept fusion under conflicting conditions.
The visibility-aware voxel masking (Appendix E) is concretely specified, including adaptive scaling with object scale and depth, which aids reproducibility.
weaknesses: The theoretical claims are overstated relative to what is actually established. The 'proof' that low-pass relaxation reduces semantic estimation error (Prop. A.4) rests on Assumptions A.2 and A.3 that essentially assume the conclusion: the semantic field is band-limited and the error is dominated by high frequencies. These are empirical conjectures about a learned neural velocity field, not verified properties, and no empirical evidence (e.g., spectral analysis of actual velocity errors) is provided to support them.

The claimed equivalence between the abstract low-pass operator on the vector field (Eq. 2) and the implemented attention-logit blurring (Eq. 8) holds only under an unverified Lipschitz-in-logits assumption (A.11). The paper markets this as a theoretical justification, but the theory-practice gap is never closed empirically, so the 'we prove' framing in the abstract and contributions is misleading.

The Wasserstein bound (Theorem A.9) is loose and generic (Gronwall-based chaining of Lipschitz constants) and provides little actionable insight; notably, the bound for RelaxFlow includes an uncontrolled δprior term, so the theorem does not actually establish that RelaxFlow is closer to ground truth — this is conceded only in a remark.

The evaluation scale is small and metric reliability is questionable: AmbiSem-3D has only 21 curated cases and ExtremeOcc-3D only 264; FID and Point-FID computed over such tiny sets are statistically fragile. The user study (n=32) reports an implausibly extreme gap (73.91% alignment vs. 4.84–11.41% for all baselines) that warrants scrutiny of study design and is not analyzed further.

The multi-prior consensus mechanism is heuristic: concatenating token sequences and relying on attention dilution is asserted (not shown) to implement consensus, and the claim that this reduces δprior is only loosely connected to the theory.

For ExtremeOcc-3D, prior images are retrieved from the same 3D-FUTURE dataset from which test cases are drawn; although different instances are sampled, the retrieval pool overlaps the test distribution in a way that is not fully controlled or discussed.

Presentation quality is uneven: the appendix contains numerous notational errors and typos (e.g., duplicated 'Let ρ = N(0, I_d)', mangled symbols like 'generallx'/'underlXing', inconsistent subscripting of X̄_t/X̂_t in Lemma A.7, Srutinize/SAM3D naming inconsistencies), which undermines confidence in the carefully-checked status of the derivations.

Baselines are not text-conditioned methods by construction, so CLIPtxt comparisons partly measure capability asymmetry rather than method quality; a stronger attempt at a text-controllable baseline (e.g., optimizing against CLIP or a direct conditioning adapter) would make the comparison more convincing.

strengths: Clear and useful problem formulation: the paper identifies a real gap—feedforward image-to-3D models collapse to 'observation-overfitted' completions under occlusion, and formalizes text-driven amodal 3D generation with two well-motivated constraints (observation fidelity vs. prompt following).

The proposed method is practical and training-free: multi-prior consensus via concatenated visual tokens, attention-logit smoothing for relaxation, a time-dependent cutoff schedule, and a visibility-aware SLAT mask. It plugs into two strong backbones (TRELLIS, SAM3D) with negligible overhead, which increases the likelihood the contribution is adopted.

Empirical evidence is reasonably comprehensive: quantitative gains on ExtremeOcc-3D across both backbones (e.g., Point-FID 100.38→81.11 on SAM3D), a user study on AmbiSem-3D (n=32), component ablations, hyperparameter sensitivity (σ, ρ, N), robustness to prior source, and efficiency discussion.

The paper introduces two new diagnostic benchmarks (ExtremeOcc-3D with 264 GT-annotated cases; AmbiSem-3D with multi-branch ambiguity), with curation details, metric definitions (Appendix D), and hyperparameter details (Appendix E) that support reproducibility.
Honest limitations treatment: the failure-case appendix (G, Fig. 11) explicitly characterizes when the method degrades (conflicting observation/prior evidence), which is commendable.
weaknesses: The central theoretical claim is overstated. The abstract claims to 'prove that our relaxation is equivalent to applying a low-pass filter on the generative vector field,' but the implementation blurs cross-attention logits, and the link between logit smoothing and velocity-field filtering is only asserted to be 'analogous' (Appendix A.4) and rests on an unverified Lipschitz-in-logits assumption (A.11). The main analysis (A.2–A.3) also assumes the semantic field is exactly band-limited and errors are high-frequency—these are heuristic spectral-separation assumptions, not results.

The Wasserstein 'guarantee' (Theorem A.9 / Eq. 5) is not very informative: the bound includes the uncontrolled residual term δprior (the proxy prior gap), so the claimed advantage over the standard flow holds only 'provided the conditioning mismatch δprior is controlled,' which the theory never establishes. The result is essentially an upper bound that does not compare the two methods without an additional unquantified assumption.

Presentation of the theory contains numerous errors that undermine confidence: garbled notation throughout Appendix A (e.g., Lemma A.7 and Theorem A.8 statements where X̄t/X̂t collapse to Xt; 'Let ρ = N(0,Id). Let ρ = N(0,Id)' duplicated in Theorem A.8; inconsistent Esem definitions between Eq. 14/15 and Eq. 3; misspelled 'Gronwall'; typos such as 'Srutinize', 'underlXing', 'generallx').

Evaluation scale and metrics are limited. AmbiSem-3D has only 21 curated cases and the user study 32 volunteers; ExtremeOcc-3D has 264 cases from a single source (3D-FUTURE/3D-FRONT). CLIPtxt is a weak proxy for 3D prompt-following and may be partially trivial when the text names the GT category; FID/Point-FID values are very high in absolute terms, making relative comparisons harder to interpret.

Baselines for the key claim are relatively weak. The main text-based competitors are 2D-edit-then-3D pipelines and using the prior as an extra TRELLIS view; stronger text/image-conditioned 3D generation or optimization-based baselines from the related-work discussion (e.g., SDS-based methods) are not compared, so the claim that existing strategies 'cannot resolve' the tension is supported only against a narrow baseline set.

The ODE interpolation framing (Eq. 1) is presented as a principled formulation, but velocity blending of two conditional flow fields is a heuristic inference rule, not a derived probability-flow ODE; the paper does not discuss what distribution the blended field actually samples from.

The multi-prior consensus mechanism is motivated narratively ('consistent attributes receive more aggregate attention') but never analyzed or verified directly (e.g., no attention-mass measurements); its effect is only observed through end metrics.

strengths: The paper formalizes a genuinely useful and underexplored task — text-driven amodal 3D generation — and clearly articulates the two competing objectives (observation fidelity vs. prompt following) and why a uniform control granularity fails.

The proposed framework is training-free and plug-and-play on two state-of-the-art backbones (TRELLIS, SAM3D), which makes the contribution immediately useful and easy to adopt; implementation details (attention-logit smoothing Eq. 8, visibility mask Eq. 11, schedule Eq. 10, appendix F) are concrete and support reproducibility.

The evaluation is unusually thorough for this area: two curated diagnostic benchmarks, comparison against four baseline families (feedforward, 2D-completion, occlusion-aware, video/multi-view/commercial-editing pipelines), component ablations, hyperparameter sensitivity, prior-source ablation, prior-count analysis, runtime/memory measurements, and a 32-person user study. Honest failure-case analysis (Appendix H) is provided.

The core empirical claim — that RelaxFlow improves semantic alignment (CLIPtxt, Point-FID) while preserving observation fidelity (CLIPimg, LPIPS competitive with the strongest baseline) — is supported consistently across both benchmarks and both backbones, and the qualitative figures are convincing.

The idea of multi-prior consensus (diluting instance-specific details across retrieved/generated priors sharing only the intended attribute) is a simple but effective and well-motivated mechanism for the visual-token conditioning interface.
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is overclaimed. Proposition A.4 (error reduction) and Theorem A.9 (Wasserstein bound) follow almost directly from the posited spectral separation assumptions (A.2, A.3) — i.e., the conclusions largely restate the assumptions (band-limited semantic field, high-frequency error). Moreover, the implementation blurs attention logits, not the vector field, so the link between Rσ applied to v and the actual mechanism rests on an additional unverified Lipschitz-in-logits assumption (A.11); the paper would be more credible presenting this as motivating intuition rather than a 'proof'.

The comparison framing in Sec. 3.1 is somewhat artificial: the 'standard neural flow' is defined as reusing observation tokens for the prior branch, and the interpolation ODE (Eq. 1) with a particular αt schedule is itself a design choice, so the theoretical separation between 'standard' and 'RelaxFlow' does not correspond to a sharp comparison against, e.g., CFG-style composition baselines in the experiments (the TRELLIS text+image CFG baseline is only in Appendix E).

Benchmark scale and realism are limited: AmbiSem-3D has only 21 hand-curated cases (with a 100-case semi-automatic extension relegated to the appendix), and ExtremeOcc-3D is built from synthetic 3D-FRONT/3D-FUTURE furniture scenes; generalization to real photographs with natural occlusion is not evaluated.

Absolute gains on automatic metrics are modest in places (e.g., CLIPimg 0.84→0.87, CLIPtxt 26.29→27.23 on AmbiSem-3D), and CLIP-based metrics are known to be coarse proxies for semantic controllability; the user study mitigates this but covers only the 21-case set.

Prior images for ExtremeOcc-3D are retrieved from the same dataset (3D-FUTURE) used to construct the ground truth, raising a mild distributional-leakage concern; the generated-prior ablation (82.7 vs. 81.1) partly addresses it, but the effect on baseline comparisons (which also receive these priors) is not fully disentangled.

Appendix proofs contain notational inconsistencies (e.g., Eq. 21 describes the prior-conditioned flow but is labeled a 'Gaussian blur flow'; Lemma A.7 mixes L_t^nn and L̃_t^nn; Theorem A.8's Minkowski step is sketched rather than derived), and several cited works are dated 2025–2026 preprints/submissions, which weakens the evidential grounding of some related-work claims.

strengths: The task formalization of text-driven amodal 3D generation is well-motivated and clearly articulated: the observation fidelity vs. prompt-following tension, and the decoupling of control granularities, is a genuinely useful framing.
RelaxFlow is training-free and plug-and-play on two modern backbones (TRELLIS, SAM3D), which increases practical utility and lowers barriers to adoption.

Two new diagnostic benchmarks (ExtremeOcc-3D, AmbiSem-3D) with a clearly described curation protocol address a real evaluation gap; the appendix details occlusion-ratio computation, ambiguity taxonomy, and a 100-case extension.

The evaluation is broader than typical: ablations on components and hyperparameters, prior-source ablation, additional baseline families (video-generation, multi-view, commercial 2D editing, direct text+image conditioning), a user study, runtime/memory reporting, and an honest failure-case section (Fig. 16, Appendix H).
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is weak relative to its billing. Proposition A.4 rests on two untestable, essentially hand-waved assumptions (A.2: the 'ideal semantic field' is band-limited; A.3: error is high-frequency) and the analysis only covers a Gaussian-blurred velocity field, whereas the implementation blurs attention logits; the bridge between them is another unverified Lipschitz assumption (A.11). The Wasserstein 'guarantee' (Thm. A.8/A.9) is only a bound whose tightness is never assessed, and the claimed tighter bound for RelaxFlow over the standard flow additionally requires δprior to be small, which is not established. The appendix also contains notation errors and inconsistencies (e.g., Eq. 14/15 define E_obs/E_sem with mismatched conditioning c_obs vs. c_sem; Theorem A.8 states 'Let ρ = N(0, Id)' twice; distinguishing X_t, X̄_t, X̂_t in the derivations is difficult), suggesting limited rigor.

Potential evaluation leakage: on ExtremeOcc-3D, prior images are retrieved by sampling another object of the same category from the same dataset (3D-FUTURE) used to build the test set, effectively injecting the ground-truth category label; baselines in Table 1 that do not consume this prior are then at an inherent disadvantage on CLIPtxt and Point-FID.

Small-scale, statistically fragile evaluation: 264 test cases for FID/Point-FID (FID with a few hundred samples is highly unreliable), and only 21 cases in AmbiSem-3D with n=32 user-study participants. Several headline improvements are small (e.g., CLIPtxt 27.23 vs. 27.41 for Nano Banana Pro on AmbiSem-3D, where 'Ours' is not even best; CLIPtxt gains in Table 1 are ~1–3 points).

Component ablations show modest effects: removing low-pass relaxation only moves Point-FID from 81.1 to 87.1, and the paper does not isolate the contribution of multi-prior consensus quantitatively, so the relative importance of the three advertised components is unclear.

The core empirical claim—low-pass relaxation stabilizes semantic guidance—is only validated end-to-end via Point-FID; there is no direct evidence (e.g., spectral analysis of the induced vector field, attention statistics, or trajectory-divergence measurements) that the mechanism operates as theorized, leaving theory and practice weakly connected.

Reproducibility is limited: no code or data release is mentioned, the benchmarks depend on manual curation (three annotators, manual filtering of 20/120 candidates), and prompt-engineering details for baseline pipelines (e.g., the long Wan2.2 prompt in Fig. 10) raise fairness questions about whether all baselines received comparable tuning effort.
Overhead is nontrivial (1.8–2.5× runtime), yet the paper does not discuss when this trade-off is justified relative to simply fine-tuning or using a text-conditioned generator.

strengths: The paper formalizes a genuinely interesting and practically relevant problem — text-driven amodal 3D generation — and the dual-granularity observation (rigid control for visible evidence vs. relaxed control for prompt intent) is a clear, well-motivated insight.
The framework is training-free and plug-and-play across two established backbones (TRELLIS, SAM3D), which increases its usefulness and lowers the barrier for others to adopt it.

The experimental package is broad: two curated diagnostic benchmarks (ExtremeOcc-3D with 264 cases, AmbiSem-3D with a 21-case set plus a 100-case extension), comparisons against multiple baseline families (occlusion-aware feedforward models, 2D-edit-then-3D, video/multi-view generation, direct text+image fusion), a user study (n=32), component ablations, hyperparameter sensitivity, prior-source ablation, and runtime/memory reporting.
The visibility-aware, time-varying fusion (Eq. 9-11) is a sensible design, and the ablation shows it is the most critical component (Point-FID 81.1 vs. 92.3 without the mask).

The limitations discussion is comparatively honest: the failure-case appendix (conflicting observation/prior conditions, 'soft concept fusion' behavior) and the note that AmbiSem-3D is intentionally multi-solution are appreciated.
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is weaker than advertised. The headline claim ('we prove that our relaxation is equivalent to a low-pass filter on the generative vector field') rests on unverified idealizations: Assumption A.2 (semantic signal is band-limited) and Assumption A.3 (estimation error is dominated by high frequencies) are posited, not empirically validated, and the implementation (attention-logit blurring) connects to the analyzed operator only via a further Lipschitz assumption (A.11). As written, the result is close to circular: given spectral separation, Gaussian filtering reduces error is essentially a restatement of the assumption. The Wasserstein bound in Eq. (5) also contains an unquantified δprior term, so 'provably tighter' holds only when the prior mismatch is small — a condition never measured.

Mechanism novelty is incremental. Blurring attention logits as guidance has been analyzed in prior work (Hong, 2024, which the authors cite), and the dual-branch velocity blending with a time-dependent schedule is a natural extension of CFG-style composition. The main novel elements are the problem formulation and the visibility mask.

There is a potential evaluation bias on ExtremeOcc-3D: prior images are retrieved as 'a different object of the same category from the 3D-FUTURE dataset' — the same dataset that provides the ground truth. Priors drawn from the ground-truth distribution could inflate Point-FID/FID gains, and a cleaner held-out prior source is only briefly reported as an ablation (82.7 vs. 81.1).

The evaluation suite relies on metrics with known weaknesses in this setting: CLIP scores are coarse for 3D semantics, FID/Point-FID computed over 264 (and 21-case) sets are statistically noisy, and min-LPIPS against a single observed view is a weak fidelity check. The user study is small (32 raters, 21 cases).

The multi-prior consensus module is heuristic — concatenating prior token sequences into cross-attention — with no analysis of why aggregate attention dilutes idiosyncratic details, and Figure 6b shows performance is sensitive to N in ways that are only empirically characterized.

The runtime overhead is substantial (2.46x on SAM3D), which the paper acknowledges but does not address; the practical trade-off relative to simpler 2D-edit baselines (e.g., Nano Banana Pro + 3D is close on CLIPtxt and Point-FID) deserves more discussion.
Reproducibility of the benchmarks is uncertain: curation pipelines are described but no explicit release commitment for ExtremeOcc-3D/AmbiSem-3D or code is stated in the manuscript.
